messages.author: ccc9ef0ed787e008
messages.subject: Generalized Linear Mixed Model
parts:
Dear all,

I'm carrying out an analysis on future time expressions in English on the basis of a corpus of spoken English. I am using a generalized linear mixed effects model (glmer) because when I coded the data I realized that there is considerable variation across conversations concerning the choice of future markers. I have a model consisting of a categorical dependent variable (future time marker WILL or BE GOING TO), a number of independent variables (syntactic, semantic and extralinguistic variables) as fixed effects, and the variable File as a random effect . Not all of my independent variables show a significant effect on the choice of future marker. My questions now are:

1. Is the procedure at arriving at a minimal adequate model the same as for logistic regression models (glm)?
2. How do I find out whether there is reason to assume overdispersion?
3. How do I find out whether my models (both the initial and the final model) have predictive power?
4. How do I determine whether variability within File is stronger than the fixed effects?

I am grateful for any comment on my questions!!
Thanks
Agnes

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] Generalized Linear Mixed Model
parts: Some brief responses from on the road, I hope others can contribute some more.
> 1. Is the procedure at arriving at a minimal adequate model the same as for logistic regression models (glm)?
There are probably as many opinions out there on that as there are references. I like the procedure outlined in Zuur et al., Ch. 5.
> 2. How do I find out whether there is reason to assume overdispersion?
My thoughts on that are just unvalidated hunches so I prefer not to put them into print. And hope someone else has more definite things to say.
> 3. How do I find out whether my models (both the initial and the final model) have predictive power?

You can compute all the regular things there: classification accuracy, the C-score, and there is now also a proposal out there on how to compute R-squareds for mixed-effects models. I don't have the reference here but google "rsquared.glmm" and you will find it (with code).
> 4. How do I determine whether variability within File is stronger than the fixed effects?

That is probably a quite tricky question because of this issue of bringing the two different types of effects together (fixed vs random). You can get some impression of the variability accounted for by the random effects from the summary output of glmer and the larger the variance, the more the random effect does. (In fact I just completed two papers on multi-level modeling taking at least a bit about that.) It is not clear to me, though, how one can make principled comparisons between fixed and random effects: the latter are not even estimated coefficients of the same type in the model ...
For mixed-effects modeling questions R-lang is probably the more useful list so you may want to try them, too.

Cheers,
STG

messages.author: ccc9ef0ed787e008
messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] Generalized Linear Mixed Model
parts:
Thank you very much for your comments. About finding out whether fixed effects or random effects is stronger: Actually I want to show that one group of my speakers shows more variability in the use of future time markers than the other. The groups (actually 2 different varieties of English) serve as fixed effects predictors, the individual conversations as random effects. I want to compare the results to a GLM including the same predictors, but without the random effects, and show that only when including random effects the overall variation can be explained. That is why I would also like to know which measure is the best for comparing which of the models predicts the variation more accurately. But I will try a more specialized list for questions like these. 

But I have two rather simple things that I encounter difficulties with and maybe someone has a solution:

1. I would like to change the default level in the summary of the model. E.g. it gives me the coefficients for male speakers (female is the intercept) and I would like to get the estimates for female speakers. Does anybody know how to change that?

2. In contrast to the summaries of the lrm() and glm() the summary of glmer() only gives me numbers for the individual predictor levels  instead of the names, e.g. "male" or "female". Is there a way I can change that, maybe add something to the syntax in the call?

Thanks!! Agnes

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] Generalized Linear Mixed Model
parts:
> The groups (actually 2 different varieties of English) serve as fixed effects predictors, the individual conversations as random effects. [...]
If you make the group factor a random effect, too - because they are
more varieties than the two you're testing here - then you could use a
multi-level model of the type I mentioned in the last mail and see
which level accounts for more variability. Just a thought ... Other
possibilities look at how classifications and their accuracies change
when the groups/conversations are not included.

> But I have two rather simple things that I encounter difficulties with and maybe someone has a solution:
> 1. I would like to change the default level in the summary of the model. E.g. it gives me the coefficients for male speakers (female is the intercept) and I would like to get the estimates for female speakers. Does anybody know how to change that?
see SFLWR 2 ed., p. 81ff.

> 2. In contrast to the summaries of the lrm() and glm() the summary of glmer() only gives me numbers for the individual predictor levels instead of the names, e.g. "male" or "female". Is there a way I can change that, maybe add something to the syntax in the call?

You must have done something wrong/weird because I get level names
("yes" for CONTRAST below)

print(model.01e.lmer)
[...]
Fixed Effects: [...]
CONTRASTyes
-2.439

Cheers,
STG
